clue.text: Cross-talking Liam's chance to act in Shakespearean troupe

indicators.note: letters set to act are put to work playing new roles, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: talking crossly, with ill temper, is being rude
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor called Liam is given his chance to tread the boards with a Shakespeare company.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rude Mechanicals are Bottom, Quince and the other workmen who stage the play within A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the amateur acting company of Athenian tradesmen in A Midsummer Night's Dream, a troupe of players.

clue.text: Saw the end of Raab — appreciate that's uplifting, basically

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting something up makes it read from bottom to top
'the end of' keeps only the last letter of 'Raab'

blocks.note: a saw is an old saying, a motto
the last letter of Raab
ta is British informal thanks

explanation.surface: Someone saw Dominic Raab's political career end and found it heartening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a past tense verb; it is the noun meaning a proverb. Ta is everyday British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: At bottom is an idiom meaning fundamentally, in essence, which is what basically means.

clue.text: Mountain in African country

blocks.note: ben is a Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mountain located somewhere in Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Benin is a West African nation lying between Togo and Nigeria.

clue.text: Backside clean on reflection? It's what sycophants do

indicators.note: a reflection shows a mirror image, so the word is turned back to front

blocks.note: butt is slang for the bottom
clean and pure are synonyms

explanation.surface: A question about personal hygiene, then a jibe about flatterers.
explanation.definitionFit: To butter up someone is to flatter them to win favour, exactly the habit of fawning toadies.

clue.text: Compensate for not filming

blocks.note: first meaning: to counterbalance
second meaning, read as two words: away from the film set

explanation.surface: Making up for a day when the camera is not rolling.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the answer into OFF SET, where an actor is when not filming.
explanation.definitionFit: To offset a loss is to counterbalance it; an actor off set is not currently shooting a scene.

clue.text: Reader's handiwork?

blocks.note: surface reading: craft work done by someone who reads books
setter's reading: the work of a fortune-teller who reads hands

explanation.surface: The craft produced by a keen reader.
explanation.walkthrough: Reader suggests books; here it is a palm reader, and handiwork is literally work on hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Palmistry is telling fortunes from the lines of the hand, the craft of a palm reader.

clue.text: It may be burnt — that's blooming insane!

indicators.note: something that blooms opens out into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry about something being burnt — blooming insane!
explanation.walkthrough: Blooming looks like a mild British expletive; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Burnt sienna is a classic reddish-brown pigment made by heating the earth colour sienna.

clue.text: Minister dealing with vulnerable refugees, migrants and asylum seekers from the start

indicators.note: dealing cards mixes them, so the letters are shuffled out of order
from the start asks for only the opening letter of each of these words

blocks.note: taken whole into the mix
the initial letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: A description of a Home Office minister responsible for refugees and asylum seekers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a job description, which is apt: Suella Braverman was the UK Home Secretary in charge of asylum policy.
explanation.definitionFit: Suella Braverman served as Home Secretary, a cabinet minister of the British government.

clue.text: Expecting trouble put: 'That man's no good!'

indicators.note: trouble as a verb means disturb or stir up, so these letters are disordered

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
he is the pronoun for that man
duff is British slang for useless or broken

explanation.surface: Someone braced for bother dismisses a man as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: Up the duff is British slang for pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Expecting is the euphemism for pregnant, and up the duff is the coarser slang for the same state.

clue.text: I'm going back out — get Brian under way at the centre

indicators.note: back tells us to read the collected string from its end to its start
at the centre asks for only the middle letter of each of the following words

blocks.note: middle letter of out
middle letter of get
middle letter of Brian
middle letter of under
middle letter of way

explanation.surface: Someone heads back outside, urging Brian to get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back out' reads as a phrasal verb; the words split, with back signalling the reversal and out supplying its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is a farewell, the word said on announcing that one is leaving.

clue.text: Echo understood about Narcissus finally — he loves himself

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other
finally points to the very last letter of the name before it

blocks.note: Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet
got it means understood
last letter of Narcissus

explanation.surface: A myth retold: Echo grasps at last what Narcissus is, a man in love with himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows the myth of Echo and Narcissus, who fell for his own reflection.
explanation.definitionFit: An egotist is a self-centred, conceited person, someone wrapped up in admiring himself.

clue.text: Cup tie, if lost, will be momentous

indicators.note: something lost is gone, so these letters drop out of the longer word

blocks.note: a semifinal is one of the knockout ties in a cup competition
the letters removed

explanation.surface: A football pundit warning that defeat in a cup match would be a turning point.
explanation.definitionFit: Seminal means highly influential, shaping what follows, which is close to momentous or of great consequence.

clue.text: Food? Pulses the first to get chucked out

indicators.text: the first to get chucked out
indicators.note: the opening letter is thrown away, leaving the rest of the word

blocks.note: pulses as rhythmic throbs are beats

explanation.surface: Talk of food: the lentils and beans are the first thing to be thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: Pulses next to Food suggests lentils; here it means heartbeats.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is informal slang for food, as in a café promising good eats.

clue.text: Romeo visiting club is hot stuff — capital!

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside a place, so one letter sits within another word

blocks.note: a bat is a club used in games
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
lava is molten rock

explanation.surface: A man visiting a nightclub finds it really hot — a capital time!
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks like an exclamation of approval; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bratislava is the capital city of Slovakia.

clue.text: Old folk finally see ex-PM with prison visiting

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word after it
a visitor goes inside, so one word is placed within another

blocks.note: last letter of see
Liz Truss was briefly British Prime Minister in 2022
can is slang for prison

explanation.surface: Elderly people finally get to see a former Prime Minister, with a prison visit thrown in.
explanation.definitionFit: The Etruscans were an ancient people of central Italy, absorbed by Rome, so a people of long ago.

clue.text: Old court favourite that's good to recall winning, as lesser players may sometimes do

definitions.text: as lesser players may sometimes do

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Tim Henman, the retired British tennis player who was a Wimbledon crowd favourite
ah is the sigh of satisfaction meaning that's good
a side that is up is ahead

explanation.surface: Remembering a former tennis darling winning, in a way weaker players sometimes manage.
explanation.walkthrough: Court means a tennis court: Tim Henman was the much-loved British player of the late 1990s and 2000s.
explanation.definitionFit: Poor actors, the lesser players, tend to overact, which is what ham it up means.

clue.text: Barking resident in bank grabbing boob

indicators.note: grabbing means holding onto, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: a bank is a row or tier, as of seats or keys
a boob is a blunder, to err

explanation.surface: A local of Barking, in east London, groped in a bank.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a London district, so it reads as a place; it is the dog's barking.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrier is a dog, a household resident given to barking.

clue.text: Ignoring Charlie, sought shelter, then assumed control

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to take cover is to seek shelter

explanation.surface: A soldier dodges Charlie, ducks for cover, then seizes command.
explanation.definitionFit: To take over is to assume charge or command of something.

clue.text: Politician in love trio's outed as a fake

indicators.note: outed suggests something broken out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, O
taken as written
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: An MP caught in a love triangle is exposed as a fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: An impostor is someone who pretends to be someone else, a fraud or sham.

clue.text: A little officer — that's disappointing!

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: a small amount of policeman
second meaning: British slang for not very good

explanation.walkthrough: Cop is British slang both for a policeman and, in this phrase, for value: not much cop means poor.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang for something that is mediocre and a letdown, while also literally a small helping of police.

clue.text: Herbal drink served up — it's all there

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word reads bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
all there means of sound mind

explanation.surface: A herbal infusion is brought out, with every ingredient included.
explanation.definitionFit: A tisane is an infusion of herbs or flowers, a herbal tea.

clue.text: Country bumpkin takes a wife in Scottish town

indicators.note: takes means taking in, so the outer word holds the others

blocks.note: a hick is a rustic yokel
taken as written
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A rustic gets married in a Scottish town.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawick is a town in the Scottish Borders, known for knitwear and rugby.

clue.text: I nearly forgot about one very dodgy dealer

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the abbreviation runs backwards

blocks.note: a postscript, PS, adds what the writer nearly forgot
Roman numeral one
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: Someone almost forgot about a very shady trader.
explanation.walkthrough: A spiv is a British word, from wartime black markets, for a flashy small-time crook.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiv is a shady trader in illicit or black-market goods, a crooked dealer.

clue.text: With Mike contributing, sets about puzzle

indicators.note: contributing means putting itself in, so that letter goes inside
about means turned round, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: sets and puts both mean places
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: With Mike chipping in, a group starts work on a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: To stump someone is to baffle or puzzle them.

clue.text: Does it make for lower profits?

definitions.text: Does it make for lower profits?

blocks.clueFragment: Does it make for lower profits?
blocks.note: surface reading: does this cause profits to fall?
setter's reading: a lower is something that lows, a mooing animal, which makes money for its owner

explanation.walkthrough: Lower looks like 'more low'; here it is one that lows, a cow. A cash cow brings in steady profit.
explanation.definitionFit: A cash cow is a business that yields steady income, and a cow is an animal that lows.

clue.text: 'Not so clever', old Beatty said to employer

indicators.note: said signals that the name is to be heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
the name Beatty spoken sounds like the letters of BT, the British telecoms firm
one who employs something uses it

explanation.surface: An old Beatty remarks to a boss that he is not that bright.
explanation.walkthrough: Employer looks like a boss; it means one who employs, as a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Obtuser is the comparative of obtuse, slow-witted, so it means less clever.

clue.text: Crease new material

blocks.note: a crease is a line
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: New fabric creases easily.
explanation.walkthrough: Linen is notorious for creasing, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Linen is a woven fabric made from flax, a textile.

clue.text: Working comrades taking a drink

indicators.note: working means set in motion and reorganised, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the main letters to rearrange
taken as written and added to the mix

explanation.surface: Fellow workers having a drink after their shift.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream soda is a sweet vanilla-flavoured fizzy soft drink.
